summary: A pre-publication draft of the revised Internet Protocol Security Option, as approved by the Protocol Standards Steering Group and provided for information. The final text was to be published as a change to MIL-STD 1777. It was replaced by RFC 1108.

eli5.summary: Some packets are secret and need a label saying how secret. This memo drafts a standard label that can be stuck on each packet.

subtitle: Labeling packets with security classifications and protection authorities

tldr.problem: Classified information transmitted over networks needs labels indicating its security level and which authorities control its protection.
tldr.mechanism: IP packets can carry optional security labels showing the classification level (Top Secret, Secret, Confidential, or Unclassified) and which National Access Programs must protect the data.
tldr.outcome: This was a draft of the revised standard but was made obsolete by RFC 1108, which provides an updated specification.

today: RFC 1038 is a draft specification that was superseded by RFC 1108, which provides the current specification for IP security options. It was intended as informational documentation for the MIL-STD 1777 standard and is not used for new implementations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1038 is a pre-publication draft of the revised Internet Protocol Security Option. It reflects the version as approved by the Protocol Standards Steering Group and was provided for informational purposes. The final version was to be published as a change to MIL-STD 1777, the military Internet Protocol standard.

The security option allows accredited trusted components of the Internet to label datagrams with security classifications and accrediting authority information. This enables receiving systems to validate that datagrams are appropriate for their intended path and that all involved authorities have certified the protection measures.
sections.eli5: This memo shows how to add security labels to Internet packets so military and classified networks know how secret each packet is and who is responsible for protecting it.

sections.title: Basic Security Option Format
sections.content:
The DoD Basic Security Option (type 130) carries security information in an optional IP header field. It has a variable length with a minimum of 4 octets. The format contains three main parts:

The first part is the Classification Protection Level, an 8-bit field specifying the U.S. classification level. It is encoded as one of four values: 11011110 for Top Secret, 10101101 for Secret, 01111010 for Confidential, or 01010101 for Unclassified. The datagram is assumed to be at this level until regraded according to the procedures of all indicated protecting authorities.

The second part is the Protection Authority Flags field, which is variable length and indicates which National Access Programs have accrediting authority over the datagram's protection. Each of the first seven bits in each octet corresponds to an authority. The low-order bit of each octet signals whether additional authority octets follow.
sections.eli5: The security label has two main parts: a number showing how secret the packet is (Top Secret, Secret, Confidential, or Unclassified) and a set of flags showing which government agencies must agree before the packet can be used.

sections.title: Classification Levels and Protection Authorities
sections.content:
The RFC defines four classification levels to protect different types of information. Top Secret is the highest classification, followed by Secret, then Confidential, and finally Unclassified. Each level indicates how sensitive the information in the datagram is.

The Protection Authority Flags field identifies which National Access Programs govern the datagram's protection. Currently defined authorities include GENSER (National Access Program, less SIOP), SIOP (the sensitive intelligence program), DSCCS-SPINTCOM (signals intelligence communications), and DSCCS-CRITICOM (critical intelligence communications). Each authority manages its own set of protection rules and certification procedures.
sections.eli5: Datagrams are marked with a secret level and then with flags showing which spy agencies have authority over that information.

sections.title: Host Usage Rules
sections.content:
Different types of hosts have different rules for how they must handle the security option. Unclassified hosts that lack security certification may optionally use the option only with an unclassified classification level and the GENSER authority flag set. They must accept incoming unclassified datagrams without the option and only accept datagrams with the option if they match this configuration.

Dedicated, System-High, and Compartmented hosts accredited at a classification level higher than unclassified must use the security option on all output datagrams. The classification level must match their accreditation level, and authority flags must be set for all accrediting authorities of the host.

Multi-Level and Controlled hosts must use the option on output, with the classification level within their accredited range and flags set for all applicable authorities. On input, they may accept unlabeled datagrams if directly interfacing with an unclassified environment; such datagrams are treated as implicitly unclassified.
sections.eli5: Different computers follow different rules: secret computers must label everything they send, while less-secret ones may skip the label or use it optionally.

sections.title: Out-of-Range Handling and Extended Security
sections.content:
If a datagram arrives with a security label that does not meet the receiving host's requirements (missing a required option, wrong classification level, or inappropriate authority flags), the receiving host follows the Out-of-Range Procedure. The data field must be overwritten with ones to prevent information leakage. The host sends an ICMP parameter problem message to the originating host, with the code and pointer field set to indicate the specific problem. A trusted intermediary device (such as a security-filtered gateway) may take a different action and send a destination unreachable message if the datagram is not acceptable for the final destination.

The DoD Extended Security Option (type 133) permits additional security information beyond that in the Basic Security Option to meet the needs of registered authorities. It is optional and variable length. It consists of an authority code (8 bits) that identifies which authority specifies the additional information, followed by variable-length additional security information defined by that authority. Multiple extended security options can appear in a single datagram.
sections.eli5: If a secret packet arrives at a computer that is not allowed to see it, the computer erases the packet and sends an error message back. Secret organizations can also add extra label information if they need to.
